gap: No result ChatGPT got states how close each linkable station actually came to its rated output in a named reviewer's test (The Solar Lab: the original EcoFlow DELTA Pro, listed at 7,200 W for a linked pair, shut down at 3,500 W sustained per unit and only finished a full discharge at 3,000 W, while one DELTA Pro 3 held 3,650 W for 60 minutes and one Anker SOLIX F3800 held 5,100 W for 37 minutes), and what each station draws at idle, which a linked pair pays twice (about 20 W for a BLUETTI Apex 300 against about 80 W for an F3800).
standout_why: Compared against the two cited guide pages (thepowerstationguide.com 'How to Connect Two Portable Power Stations', 2026-09-18, and the uncited outdoorpowerreviews.com parallel-charge guide, 2026-10-29), EcoFlow's spec blog, the DELTA Pro 3 manuals and product pages, and the BLUETTI AC240P manual page. Every one gives only maker ratings (7,200 W, 8,000 W, 10,000 W, 11,520 W, 12,000 W, 14,400 W). The Power Station Guide relies on 'owner reports' with no figures, and Outdoor Power Reviews says it 'does not buy or test the products it covers'. None reports a measured sustained load, a measured usable capacity or an idle draw for any candidate. I also found no published text test of two linked units under load for any of the systems (Double Voltage Hub, 50 Amp Hub, Double Power Hub, Fusion Box, Hub A1, the Jackery 5000 Plus Smart Transfer Switch pair). That absence is itself new: every combined-output figure in ChatGPT's table is a maker rating that nobody has published a check of.
decides: This demotes the original EcoFlow DELTA Pro. ChatGPT lists it at 7,200 W for a linked pair, but The Solar Lab could not hold 3,500 W from one unit, so plan on about 6,000 W from two. It confirms the DELTA Pro 3 (3,650 W for an hour, 89%) and the Anker SOLIX F3800 / F3800 Plus (5,100 W for 37 min, 84%; 7,200 W for about 10 s) as pairs whose per-unit ratings held up under sustained load. Idle draw sets standby runtime for a linked pair: two Apex 300s at about 20 W each cost about 40 W, two F3800s at about 80 W each cost about 160 W, and two Jackery 5000 Plus at about 58 W each cost about 116 W. A shopper who will leave the linked system idling for outage readiness should prefer Apex 300 or the EcoFlow DELTA Pro (21 W) on that count. Usable energy also differs by reviewer and load: Notebookcheck got only 2,905 Wh (75%) from the F3800 at a 260 W draw, while OutdoorGearLab got 3,790 Wh (about 92.5%) from the DELTA Pro 3.
